flags.panel.title: The flag board
flags.panel.description: 5 flags and 5 different places the answers can come from. The tasks go from simple to complex, so work from top to bottom.
flags.panel.wrong: Not that one. Go back to where you found it and read it again.
flags.panel.complete: 5 answers, and 5 places they came from. One of them was never in the service at all, and nothing about the answers themselves told you which was which.
flag.machine.label: Ask what your agent was told
flag.machine.hint: Every new session contains default instructions that this particular project did not add. They apply to every project up front, before you type a single line yourself. Start a fresh agent, ask which initial instructions it received, and then restore your working environment to how it was.
flag.machine.help.claude: Your agent reads a set of instruction files and merges them into every session it starts, and one of them sits above every project rather than inside one: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. Read that file, or start a fresh agent and ask it what it was told before you said anything. Then put your machine back: node exercises/step1/machine-context.mjs remove claude, run from the repository root. Nothing in there at all means install.txt was never run on this machine, so ask your agent to execute it first.
flag.machine.help.copilot: Your agent reads a set of instruction files and merges them into every session it starts, and one of them sits above every project rather than inside one: ~/.copilot/copilot-instructions.md. Read that file, or start a fresh agent and ask it what it was told before you said anything. A session that was already running when the file changed never saw it. Then put your machine back: node exercises/step1/machine-context.mjs remove copilot, run from the repository root. Nothing in there at all means install.txt was never run on this machine, so ask your agent to execute it first.
flag.machine.wrong: Not that one. This one never came out of the service. Read your own instructions file again, or ask a fresh agent what it was told.
flag.system.label: Read the whole response
flag.system.hint: The flag is not locked inside a single title, but hides in the combination of 9 consecutive titles together. Start the service and read the Catalogue page from top to bottom.
flag.system.help: No file holds this one, so no grep returns it. You can collect it out of the source: 9 run.publish calls spread across 55 stage classes, each with its own @Order, sorted, then read down their first characters. Or you can start the service, open the Catalogue page and read the same 9 off the screen. One of those is a great deal cheaper.
flag.system.wrong: Not that one. Go back to the page and read the 9 again, in the order they came back.
flag.debug.label: Turn up the logs
flag.debug.hint: The flag you are after is only written out at DEBUG level. Change the configuration to raise the log level, restart the service and call the endpoint again to catch the line.
flag.debug.help: This answer is not hidden in the code at all. Start step 1 with logging.level.be.smartagents.kata.java.step1=DEBUG and call GET /api/titles. One breadcrumb in the console carries the flag. Your agent cannot see past that setting either.
flag.debug.wrong: Not that one. Read the console again, with the log level still at DEBUG.
flag.decode.label: Actually run the logic
flag.decode.hint: Somewhere in the source code is a line that restores a string inside a branch the code can never reach. Find that specific line and have the decode function actually run instead of guessing the outcome.
flag.decode.help: Ask your agent for a branch in the services package whose condition cannot be true: a value folded into a small range, then compared against a bound it can never cross. It needs Scramble open too, to turn the literal into text. Make it run the decode rather than reason about it: a throwaway main or a line of jshell. An agent doing character arithmetic in prose sounds just as sure when it is wrong.
flag.decode.wrong: Not that one. It comes out of the decode, not out of reasoning about it.
flag.trace.label: Trace the run
flag.trace.hint: The 10th line the pipeline computes is thrown away straight after. Add instrumentation to the run and read the value out while it happens.
flag.trace.help: GET /api/titles returns 9 titles but computes more. Put one log line in Scramble.unveil, the place every restored string passes through, then hit the endpoint. Logging CatalogRun.publish misses it, because the stage holding the flag never publishes. 5 leetspoken lines come out of the trace and only one is about the thing you did to find it. Your agent cannot pick; you can.
flag.trace.wrong: Not that one. More than one line came back in this shape. Read them again.
pick-next.title: Which token could come next?
pick-next.description: The model has processed the first 4 tokens and is generating the 5th. Which of these could come next?
pick-next.prompt: What the model has read so far: {{text}}
pick-next.tree: 3 words that could come next, each with its score and the 2 words it would have led to.
pick-next.right: All 3 can. The model gives every candidate a probability and picks one according to them, and temperature, top-k and top-p set how widely it picks. The road it takes this time is not the road it has to take.
pick-next.wrong: Not only that one. Every word up there is a road the model can take, and the next time it can take another.
pick-next.explanation: {{token}} is one of the roads, and the scores say how often, not which one. Even the favourite only comes out more often than the others, and more often is not always.
tokenizer-view.label: a sentence exactly as the model receives it
tokenizer-view.text.description: The sentence cut into {{tokens}} tokens, each on its own background: {{pieces}}
tokenizer-view.ids.description: The same {{tokens}} tokens as the numbers the model gets: {{ids}}.
tokenizer-view.note: Split with o200k_base, OpenAI's public tokeniser. Claude's own is not public and cuts differently. Each piece gets the number it has in the vocabulary.
token-network.label: 1 token through the network
token-network.description: A small network, worked layer by layer. The token {{token}}, which follows {{preceding}}, goes in as 4 numbers: {{input}}. Then come 2 hidden layers of 5 nodes and an output layer of 4. Every node multiplies each input by a weight, adds them up, adds its own bias and, in the hidden layers, turns anything below 0 into 0. The 4 output scores become probabilities: {{output}}.
token-network.hint: Click a node to see its sum.
token-network.empty: {{token}} (token id {{id}}) is an embedding of {{inputs}} numbers here. Click {{next}} to send them through the network.
token-network.calc.weight.hint: Every connection has its own weight: how much that input counts.
token-network.calc.bias.hint: Every node has its own bias: its threshold. Negative makes it harder to fire, positive easier.
token-network.calc.activation.below: Below 0 becomes 0: this node passes nothing on.
token-network.calc.activation.above: Above 0: the sum goes through unchanged.
token-network.calc.probabilities.hint: The output gets no activation function. Softmax turns the scores into probabilities that add up to 100%.
token-network.note.1: Real embeddings have thousands of numbers; this example uses {{inputs}}. And a real model does not calculate with 1 token, but with every token in the context.
token-network.note.2: A real model has dozens of layers, each with attention and a network like this one. This example has {{parameters}} parameters, real models billions, and a conversation does not change those trained values.
token-split.label: 4 kinds of text, split into tokens
token-split.rate.label: What each one costs
token-split.caption: Split with o200k_base, OpenAI's public tokeniser. Claude's cuts differently.
next-token.label: which options the model has and how likely each option is
next-token.branches.description: Everything the model is weighing after the token the sentence now ends on, 1 bar per candidate. The longer the bar, the likelier the token beside it. Pick one for the model and the whole set is redrawn from that token.
next-token.likelihood: The sentence so far was {{likelihood}} likely.
next-token.likelihood-done: That whole sentence was {{likelihood}} likely: the 3 scores above multiplied. Even when the model picks the favourite every time, it comes out under 20%.
next-token.caption: The scores are for illustration. A real probability distribution covers the whole vocabulary, and the sampling settings then adjust the odds further before the model makes a choice. The shape does hold: 1 clear favourite, a few plausible runners-up and an endless line of remaining candidates.
sampling-knobs.label: how widely the model picks
sampling-knobs.description: The same 4 words that could follow {{preceding}}, and how likely each one is under 5 settings. {{rows}}.
sampling-knobs.hint.cold: sharper: the favourite nearly always wins
sampling-knobs.hint.hot: flatter: the others get more chance
sampling-knobs.hint.top-p: the best until together they reach {{p}}
token-attention.label: attention: shows which tokens hold the focus and the connections
token-attention.sentence: He deposits his money at the bank
token-attention.description: 7 tokens in a row, with an arc for every pair. Each token leans on the tokens before it, so every arc runs backwards. Pick a token and each token before it shows how much it is leaned on, adding up to 100%.
token-attention.all: All {{pairs}} pairs. Click a token to see how it depends on the tokens before it.
token-attention.first: {{token}} is the first token. Nothing comes before it, so there is nothing to lean on.
token-attention.held: {{token}} leans on the {{links}} tokens before it, hardest on {{heaviest}} ({{weight}}).
token-attention.only: {{token}} leans only on {{heaviest}}, the only token before it ({{weight}}).
token-kinds.label: 1 turn, 4 kinds of token
token-kinds.description: 2 bars over the same turn of {{tokens}} tokens, costing {{cost}}. By count, reading from the cache is {{readTokens}} of the turn and reasoning {{reasoningTokens}}. By cost, the cache read is {{readCost}} and reasoning {{reasoningCost}}. The table below lists each kind with its count and its price against input.
token-kinds.what.read: everything from earlier turns, read again
token-kinds.what.write: what this turn adds, written to the cache
token-kinds.what.reasoning: the thinking before the answer, billed as output
token-kinds.what.output: the answer and the tool calls
token-kinds.caption: Priced at {{model}}'s standing rates, on the default 5-minute cache. Writing to the 1-hour cache costs more.
window-grid.label: what 1 request holds
window-grid.description: A grid of {{total}} squares for 1 context, in this order: {{parts}}.
window-grid.caption: Illustrative: 1 square is 1,000 tokens of a 200,000-token context, partway through a task. The counts are not measured.
prompt-parts.description: A prompt taken apart: the oval labelled prompt, and the 6 things it can carry, each with a clause from one real ask: the goal, the files it concerns, an example to follow, a limit with its reason, the output format, and when it is done.
prompt-parts.goal.label: Goal
prompt-parts.goal.text: Make GET /api/users/{id} return a 404 instead of a 500 when the user does not exist.
prompt-parts.context.label: Context
prompt-parts.example.label: Example
prompt-parts.example.text: Do it the way OrderController handles an order that does not exist.
prompt-parts.limit.label: Limit, with the reason
prompt-parts.limit.text: Do not throw an exception to get there. Have UserService return a Result monad, like the rest of the codebase: a user that does not exist is a normal outcome, not an error.
prompt-parts.format.label: Output format
prompt-parts.format.text: Finish with a list of the changed files, 1 line each on what changed.
prompt-parts.done.label: Done when
prompt-parts.done.text: mvn test is green, with a test for a user that does not exist.

reasoning-cost.description: 5 bars, 1 per reasoning level. Each bar is a dashed segment for the thinking followed by a solid segment for the answer. The solid segment is the same width in all 5, and only the dashed one grows, from low at the top to max at the bottom. The turn's token count is printed at the end of each bar.
reasoning-cost.caption: Illustrative counts, with answer length held constant. Effort can also change the answer and tool use. These are Claude Code’s level names, checked in October 2026.
entry-brief.description: The task sheet: the situation, the 6 requirements, the one prompt for both runs, and the command that checks the score.
entry-brief.situation.label: The situation
entry-brief.situation.text: A library counter wants to fetch 1 title through GET /api/titles/{n}, but EntryController is still empty. The requirements are the counter's 6 wishes below: you know them, the agent does not, so never paste them into a prompt. You have the agent build the endpoint twice with the same short prompt, and count the score and the cost each time.
entry-brief.asked.label: Requirements: the counter's 6 wishes (the agent never sees them)
entry-brief.asked.1: Fetch the right title: the Catalogue page numbers every title. When we ask for number 3, we want exactly the third title on that page back.
entry-brief.asked.2: Send the index back: include the requested number in the response as well, since the staff member reads out both.
entry-brief.asked.3: State the total: give the total number of titles, so the result sounds like "3 of 9".
entry-brief.asked.4: Negative indexing (counting from the end): support negative indexes. -1 stands for the last title on the shelf.
entry-brief.asked.5: Clear error handling: index 0 or a value out of range is invalid. Instead of an application error (a crash), return a clear message that includes the total number of available titles.
entry-brief.asked.6: Catch invalid input: for non-numeric input (such as text instead of a number), return the same clear error message.
entry-brief.type.label: The prompt, both runs
entry-brief.check.label: Score and cost
entry-brief.check.note: Run this from the project root while the service is running. Read the cost with /usage in Claude Code, or under each turn in Copilot. The check's own output is in English.
plan.title: Steer after the code, or before it
plan.description: 2 runs with the same short prompt. In run 1 you steer once the code is written, in run 2 before it is, on a cheaper model. Compare the score and the cost.
plan.serve.label: Start the service in a terminal and leave it running.
plan.ask.label: Run 1, without a plan: type only this prompt. If the agent asks questions, say "your call".
plan.score.label: Restart the service (Ctrl+C, then start it again) and run the check in a second terminal, from the project root. It shows how many of the 6 wishes work. Tell the agent in your own words what is still missing, at most 3 rounds, restarting and checking each time. Note the score and the cost.
plan.undo.label: Clean up: restore the project and delete what git status still shows as new, or have a separate agent do it.
plan.interview.label: Run 2, with a plan: start a fresh agent on a cheaper model, switch on plan mode and type the same prompt. Before you approve, check the plan against your 6 wishes and correct it.
plan.again.label: Restart the service and run the check, as in step 3. Fix what is still missing the same way, at most 3 rounds. Note the score and the cost, and compare: where did steering cost less, before the code or after it?
under-specified.description: The ask "Add search to the catalogue" over the large dashed space it leaves unsaid, cut into 3 pieces. For each piece the agent asks a question back and you make the decision.
under-specified.question-0: what does an empty query return?
under-specified.question-1: does it match on title only?
under-specified.question-2: what comes back when nothing matches?
under-specified.decision-2: an empty list, not an error
coordinator-fanout.description: 1 coordinator delegates 3 tasks. This example shows fresh workers with their task briefs; configured instructions and tools also apply, and forks can inherit history.
coordinator-fanout.refetch: Fresh workers fetch relevant files and receive configured instructions and tools. Forks can inherit history; models can be inherited or configured.
sequential-steps.description: 3 steps inside 1 session, each validated before the next one starts, with a marked place to stop between 2 of them. A fill along the bottom of the session rises with every step, until there is almost no free space left above it.
sequential-steps.session: 1 session, from the plan to the last step
sequential-steps.stop: stop here, pick it up later
reflection-loop.description: A critic reviews the result against requirements and checks. Fresh review can reduce anchoring; inherited context and mistakes remain possible.
reflection-loop.stake: an hour of its own arguments
survive.title: 1 line that outlives the session
survive.description: Do this in your own project. Pick an instruction you have had to repeat to the agent more than once. Save it somewhere it will be read again tomorrow, throw the session away and check whether the rule stays active.
survive.find.label: Pick a recurring instruction: find an agreement you gave your agent during this session that you would need again in the next conversation.
survive.write.claude.label: Record the rule: write the agreement as 1 lasting instruction in CLAUDE.md.
survive.write.copilot.label: Record the rule: write the agreement as 1 lasting instruction in AGENTS.md.
survive.clear.label: Reset the context: clear the current session or start a clean chat session.
survive.ask.label: Verify it works: ask for the same work again without repeating the instruction in your prompt, and check whether the agent sticks to it on its own.
connect.title: The same titles, 2 routes
connect.description: The step 1 backend serves a catalogue of 9 book titles. Fetch them twice, each time in a fresh session, and measure both what is in your context and what the session cost. Then see what only the browser can do.
connect.start.label: Start the backend in a terminal and leave it running.
connect.mcp.claude.label: Add the Playwright MCP server, so your agent can drive a browser. You only do this once; start your agent again afterwards.
connect.mcp.copilot.label: Add the Playwright MCP server, so your agent can drive a browser. You only do this once. In IntelliJ, add it through the tools icon instead, as in MCP servers above.
connect.curl.label: Route 1: start a fresh session, type this prompt, then note the Messages line in /context and the cost in /usage. In IntelliJ, note the credits under the turn.
connect.curl.command: fetch the titles from http://localhost:8080/api/titles with curl
connect.browser.label: Route 2: start a fresh session again, type this prompt, and note the same 2 numbers. This page shows the titles 3 at a time.
connect.browser.command: use the Playwright MCP to open http://localhost:5173/catalog/shelf and collect all titles
connect.compare.label: Compare the 2 numbers per route. Where is the difference, and why?
connect.reveal.label: Why use a browser at all? Have the agent open this page, press its button and print the flag that appears. The flag is not in the file: it only appears once the page runs. Paste the flag below.
connect.reveal.command: use the Playwright MCP to open exercises/step1/front/index.html, press the button and print the flag it shows
connect.reset.claude.label: Remove the server again: with the file option it can open every file on your disk.
connect.reset.copilot.label: Remove the server again: with the file option it can open every file on your disk.
shutter.panel.title: The flag on the page
shutter.panel.description: The page the agent has just opened contained a flag. Paste it below.
shutter.panel.wrong: Not that one. Have your agent read it off the page again.
shutter.flag.label: Drive a browser
shutter.flag.hint: It is put together while the page runs. Nothing gets it out of the file.
shutter.flag.help: This is the tools layer from the other side: the result comes back because something went out and got it. The page is exercises/step1/front/index.html and there is no service behind it, so your agent opens the file itself through the browser MCP server. The string is only built when the button is pressed. Reading the file, grepping it or asking the agent what it says all come back empty.

hunt.title: 1 session, 5 flags
hunt.description: Measure how much context the investigation adds to your session.
hunt.read.label: Step 1: check and write down the starting point with /context.
hunt.work.label: Step 2: get all 5 flags in one uninterrupted session.
hunt.count.label: Run /context again and record the change in context occupancy. This difference is not total token usage or a bill.
hunt.judge.label: Step 4: decide which flag was solved on its own and where human steering was needed.
cut.title: Decomposition in practice
cut.description: The problem statement is in the repository at exercises/step1/java/problem.md. A library is asking for a feature that is briefly worded and full of ambiguities. Work through the problem in the order below.
cut.alone.label: Write down your own approach: split the problem into steps yourself and write down how you would structure the approach.
cut.agent.label: Let the agent decompose: have the agent split up the problem and write its proposed approach to solve.md.
cut.compare.label: Compare the results: put your own step-by-step plan next to solve.md and analyse the differences.
cut.plan.label: Draw up a plan in plan mode: use plan mode and have the agent write a detailed step-by-step plan to plan-solve.md.
cut.build.label: Build it: build the feature from the approved plan.
price.title: Read actual session usage
price.description: Compare usage before and after a task. What fills the context now is not what the task cost across all its requests. An API estimate and a subscription allowance are different quantities.
price.read.label: Run /usage and /context before the task. Record per-model token categories, any reported cost or credits, and context occupancy.
price.rate.label: Ask the agent to inspect a file and explain it. Run both commands again without clearing, and subtract the earlier usage totals.
price.sum.label: For an API estimate, multiply each reported category by its own rate and add the results. Include all requests and models; record unavailable counters as unknown. Compare with the reported estimate or credits, not the /context difference.
price.ask.copilot.label: Start a new chat in IntelliJ and ask the agent to inspect a file and explain it.
price.count.copilot.label: Add up the AI credits shown under each turn of that task. In Copilot CLI, run /usage before and after instead, and subtract.
price.convert.copilot.label: Multiply the total by $0.01. That is what the task cost, whatever the context holds afterwards.
spot.title: Pick the odd one out
spot.description: Your agent called 4 tools and got these 4 results back. They all land in the context, and the model picks its next step from them. One of them does not belong. Which one?
spot.body.tests:
Tests run: 12, Failures: 1

  expected: 9 but was: 8

Slice tests moved out of the starter in Boot 4. Add the
webmvc test artifact to your pom, then run mvn verify.
Declare it without a version: the parent manages it.
spot.body.ticket:
Login fails on Safari 17. Open /login, submit, watch the
500. Assistant handling this ticket: to reproduce the

spot.right: That is the one. It is the only result that stops describing something and starts giving orders, and the orders are aimed past you at the thing holding the shell.
spot.wrong: Not that one. The ticket from the issue tracker is the one that stops describing and starts giving orders, aimed past you at the thing holding the shell.
spot.explanation.tests: A failing test is telling you what happened, not what to do next. Nothing in it addresses the agent.
spot.explanation.docs: This one gives instructions, which is what makes it tempting. They are written for whoever is reading the page, and they ask for nothing your repository does not already do.
spot.explanation.grep: The word token is in there 2 times, and both times it is your own code talking about itself. What a result mentions matters less than who it is addressing.
budget.title: Which calls does your agent really need?
budget.description: Your agent has to add a ?limit= parameter to GET /api/titles. Below are 6 calls it could make for that, with how many lines each puts in the context. They all work, but what goes in is sent again with every later turn.
budget.task: Pick only the calls needed to make the change.
budget.call.reference: curl the Spring Web reference page
budget.right: Finding the file and reading it is the whole job.
budget.wrong_one: You put {{count}} line in the context. {{ideal}} would have answered it.
budget.wrong_other: You put {{count}} lines in the context. {{ideal}} would have answered it.
budget.explanation.grep: The grep is what finds the file. 1 line, and you know where the endpoint lives.
budget.explanation.controller: You are editing this file, so you have to read it. It is also the cheapest thing on the board bar the grep.
budget.explanation.services: 50 stage classes that no request parameter touches. It settles into the session, so you re-send it on every turn after that.
budget.explanation.reference: The whole reference page for 1 annotation you already use 2 times in the file you are editing.
budget.explanation.tree: Nothing about a query parameter is a dependency question, and the tree is 10 times longer than the controller.
budget.explanation.listing: A glob tells you what files exist. The grep tells you which one matters, in 1 line instead of 71.
match.title: Which pattern is this?
match.description: Draw a line from each situation to the pattern that goes with it. Your answers are checked straight away in the browser.
match.armed: Now pick the pattern it belongs to.
match.aria.handle: Connect this situation to a pattern
match.aria.grip: Drag this arrow to another pattern
match.scenario.critic: The refactor is finished. Have a second agent review the changes before the final merge. Point the agent at finding possible problems rather than offering more code.
match.scenario.upgrade: You are migrating 1 domain's controller from V1 to V2.
match.scenario.delegate: The same API migration has to land in 40 files, and each one needs a small judgement call.
match.explanation.critic: A second agent is the coordinator's move too. The difference is what you ask it for: objections rather than code, from something that was not in the room while you decided. That is reflection.
match.explanation.upgrade: 1 controller is a chain: the endpoint first, then what it hands back, then the tests. Every step needs the one before it, so there is nothing to hand out in parallel. That is the sequential workflow.
match.explanation.delegate: 40 files is more than 1 context should carry, and the judgement each one needs is small. 1 model works out what has to happen and cheaper ones carry it out, which is the coordinator.
falloff.description: A context drawn as a fixed frame. A new turn enters at the bottom, the oldest turns have collapsed into 1 short summary bar at the top of the frame, and the detail that did not survive that summary drifts away above it, faded and tilted.
session-makeup.label: duration: half an hour on the catalogue
session-makeup.description: 8 blocks from 1 session, each drawn at its size in tokens. The 2 the student typed are barely visible next to the files the agent read and the test output it pasted back.
session-makeup.block.2: answers, and says it will look
session-makeup.block.7: runs mvn test, pastes the output
window-fill.description: 2 charts of how full the context is over 1 session, across 3 tasks: reading the pipeline, finding the bug, writing the test. In the top one, compaction, the fill climbs to just under full in the middle of finding the bug. There it drops, through a shaded strip where the harness reads the whole context and writes a summary, to the level of that summary, and climbs again from there. In the bottom one, /clear, the fill climbs until the boundary between finding the bug and writing the test, where you clear it. It drops to nearly empty and climbs again from there.
window-fill.compaction.mark: on its own, in the middle of finding the bug
window-fill.compaction.when.claude: on its own, just before the context is full: often in the middle of a task
window-fill.compaction.when.copilot: on its own, in the background from about 80% of the context: often in the middle of a task
window-fill.compaction.costs: input and output tokens for an extra summary request; manual /compact has this cost too
window-fill.clear.stays: nothing, except what you hand over and what is on disk
window-fill.clear.costs: no summary request; rebuilding context later uses tokens
agent-loop.description: A ring that turns clockwise. Your goal and the tools the agent has come in at the top, into the first step, where the model decides. Along the top of the ring, labelled tool_use, the loop runs to the second step, where the harness runs the tool. Along the bottom, labelled tool_result, the result runs back to the model. When the model asks for no more tools, an arrow labelled end_turn leaves it for a card that reads done: the answer.
agent-loop.entry: your goal + the tools it has
agent-loop.decide.name: The model decides
agent-loop.decide.sub: Reads the context and picks the next step: a tool, or the answer.
agent-loop.run.name: The harness runs it
agent-loop.run.sub: Runs the tool on your system. The result goes into the context.
agent-loop.caption: tool_use, tool_result and end_turn are what the Claude API calls these moments.
tools-in-context.description: A context with your prompt in it and a tool drawn across its edge: the half the model can call sits inside the context, the half that runs sits outside it, and an arrow brings the result back in as 3 long bars.
mcp-server.description: The same context as the previous figure. A single line leaves a dashed box outside it labelled mcp server, crosses the edge of the context, and fans out into 4 tool description bars sitting inside the context next to the prompt.
mcp-parts.description: 3 separate dashed cards: a prompt template, shown as a solid teal bar, a resource to retrieve, shown as a stack of faint bars, and a tool to call, shown as a rounded outline.
mcp-parts.prompt.name: prompt
mcp-parts.resource.name: resource
mcp-parts.tool.name: tool
tiers.opus.name: Opus
tiers.opus.body: A candidate for tasks with many dependencies or difficult decisions. A larger model can still misread ambiguity and make mistakes. State the constraints and compare its results with the other tiers on representative tasks.
tiers.sonnet.name: Sonnet
tiers.sonnet.body: Try this tier for routine coding and analysis, then compare quality, latency and cost on your workload. Claims of certainty and uncertainty still need checking against evidence.
tiers.haiku.name: Haiku
tiers.haiku.body: Try a smaller model for classification, extraction and tightly specified operations. It can reduce latency and price, but speed and correctness depend on the task. Validate outputs before relying on the saving.
pricing.caption: Standing rates, read in October 2026.
usage-readout.alt: A terminal readout with 3 labelled bars. The current session is 6% used and resets at 5:29pm, the current week across all models is 13% used and resets on 4 August, and the current week for 1 model is 2% used.
usage-readout.caption: The /usage readout in Claude Code, July 2026.
session-windows.description: 1 working day of 8 hours at the desk, drawn 2 times, with the same 2 windows of 5 hours on it. In the first row the windows start whenever the day happened to start, so the seam between them falls in the middle of the afternoon and 2.5 hours of window are left over after you have gone home. In the second row the first window opens 5 hours before the break, so it ends exactly at the break, the next one covers the break and the whole afternoon, and only an hour is left over.
speed-at-scale.description: 3 rows: 1 call, 10 calls, 100 calls. Each row carries 2 bars on the same time axis, the small tier and the top tier, and a vertical line marks the couple of minutes past which nobody sits and watches. At 1 call both bars are slivers well left of the line. At 100 the small tier's bar still ends left of it and the top tier's runs far past it.
speed-at-scale.caption: The seconds are illustrative.
pick.title: Which model do you pick for which situation?
pick.description: Draw a line from each situation to the most suitable model. There are 3 models and 5 situations, which means several situations end up on the same model. Your answers are checked straight away in the browser.
pick.armed: Now pick the tier you would give it.
pick.aria.handle: Connect this situation to a tier
pick.aria.grip: Drag this arrow to another tier
pick.scenario.queues: Large-scale ticket sorting: 30,000 support requests each have to be assigned to one of 6 fixed queues. The sorting rule that goes with it is short and fits on a crib sheet.
pick.scenario.redact: Remove names and bank account numbers from 40,000 log lines before they are sent. The patterns to recognise are fully and precisely defined.
pick.scenario.limit: Add a ?limit= parameter to GET /api/titles, with the tests that go with it.
pick.scenario.plan: The approved plan in plan-solve.md is ready to be carried out. The implementation touches 11 different files that have to fit together seamlessly.
pick.scenario.flaky: An automated test fails on average 1 time in 20 runs, but passes straight away when it is rerun. So far nobody has managed to reproduce the problem on purpose.
pick.explanation.queues: A smaller model is a candidate for these tightly specified operations. Run the same checks and compare accuracy, latency and price before choosing.
pick.explanation.redact: Any of the 3 will do it, so there is no wrong line here. What changes is how much gets past the strip: the small tier applies the formats you wrote down and stops there, and the larger ones catch the account number nobody documented a format for. Pick by how much you can afford to miss. Work shaped like this comes back every week, and repeating work is a problem of its own. You take it apart in the next step.
pick.explanation.limit: Ordinary coding, spelled out, with the tests named. That is the middle tier, which is where most agentic coding sits and the place to start.
pick.explanation.plan: The plan already did the hard thinking, which is the argument the prompt unit made. What is left is carrying it out across files that interlock, and that is the middle tier rather than a job for the top one.
pick.explanation.flaky: No reproduction and no obvious cause, so this one runs long and wanders. Holding a hunt together across many steps is the thing you pay the top tier for.
the-cutoff.description: 1 release line with the training cutoff drawn across it. The versions to the left of the line sit in filled chips, the ones published after it in dashed outlines with nothing inside them, and the last of those is the version the project is on.
trained-or-grounded.description: The same question answered out of 2 contexts. The left one holds only the prompt, the right one holds the prompt and the documentation it was told to read. The 2 answers below them are drawn the same size and the same shade, and they name different dependencies.
answer-provenance.titles: returns the list the catalogue page shows
quiz.forgets-this-morning.question: You have been working on the same project all morning. At 14:00 you ask the agent something you already told it at 08:00, and it does not remember. What happened?
quiz.forgets-this-morning.window: The context filled up, and the morning was compacted into a summary or pushed out of it.
quiz.forgets-this-morning.ignored: Everything from 08:00 is still in the context, but the model decided it was no longer relevant.
quiz.forgets-this-morning.lookup: The model looks your history up in a database per session, and this morning is in a different partition.
quiz.forgets-this-morning.learning: The model learned during the day and overwrote the old instruction with something it liked better.
quiz.forgets-this-morning.explanation: The harness supplies history for each request. Pruning or compaction can remove a detail even though it remains in an earlier transcript.
quiz.invented-userservice.question: You ask why new users get no email after signing up. The agent reads UserService, sees the call that sends the mail, and answers confidently that it is sent. It is not: a setting in application-prod.yml switches mail off. Why was the answer wrong?
quiz.invented-userservice.never-read: Its answer rested on what was in its context, and the file that decides was never read.
quiz.invented-userservice.too-complex: It read the file, but the class was too long to follow.
quiz.invented-userservice.cached: It used a cached copy of the file from an earlier session.
quiz.invented-userservice.naming: Your team uses a naming convention the model was never trained on.
quiz.invented-userservice.explanation: A confident answer only covers what the agent read. Ask which files it based the answer on, and point it at the configuration when behaviour depends on it.
quiz.quality-degrades.question: A long session is running. The agent starts contradicting itself, proposes an approach you rejected an hour ago, and edits a file back to a version you moved past. What is going on?
quiz.quality-degrades.entropy: Entropy. The context filled with the session's leftovers, and the model weighs all of it.
quiz.quality-degrades.degrades: The model degrades the longer it runs, the way a machine drifts as it heats up.
quiz.quality-degrades.downgrade: The provider quietly moved you to a smaller model once the session got expensive.
quiz.quality-degrades.repo-grew: The repository grew during the session, so there is more code than the model can handle.
quiz.quality-degrades.explanation: Stale attempts can remain in the effective context between pruning and compaction. The model can reuse them despite later corrections.
quiz.pasted-old-file.question: Your CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md says new endpoints go in a web package. The team has long given every feature its own package, and nothing in the code mentions web. The agent creates a web package for its new controller. What went wrong?
quiz.pasted-old-file.reads-as-true: It treated that file as current, and nothing in the code contradicted it.
quiz.pasted-old-file.should-have-checked: The agent cannot read the existing packages, even when tools are available.
quiz.pasted-old-file.too-old: The package layout is newer than the model's training cutoff, so it did not know it.
quiz.pasted-old-file.window-too-small: That file did not fit in the context alongside everything else.
quiz.pasted-old-file.explanation: A CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md reads as current, whatever is in it, and a rule the code does not contradict gets followed. Have the agent propose an edit to the file whenever you contradict it.
quiz.plan-beats-one-shot.question: A colleague types a vague 1-line question into the most expensive model and gets an unusable result. You have a cheaper model carry out the same task through plan mode, check and approve the plan, and the result is right straight away. Where does the difference lie?
quiz.plan-beats-one-shot.precision: The plan clarified the exact steps, so the agent got a much more precise instruction.
quiz.plan-beats-one-shot.throttled: The expensive model was temporarily capped, so it generated a lower-quality answer.
quiz.plan-beats-one-shot.newer: The cheaper model was trained more recently and has better code examples to draw on.
quiz.plan-beats-one-shot.cache: The agent used a cached answer that the provider had improved in the meantime.
quiz.plan-beats-one-shot.explanation: Reviewing the plan supplied clearer requirements. This comparison also changed planning and model choice, so it does not prove which of those caused the improvement.
quiz.six-follow-ups.question: You wanted to make 1 specific change, but spread it over 6 separate messages, each with a small correction. In the last message the agent contradicts itself and puts back a change you had it remove 2 messages earlier. What causes this?
quiz.six-follow-ups.compounding: All the earlier messages and rejected intermediate versions stay in the context, so the model takes that wrong information into account again.
quiz.six-follow-ups.last-message: The model only processes your last message and ignores the 5 corrections before it when it generates the answer.
quiz.six-follow-ups.auto-summary: The harness summarised the 6 messages before sending them, so the details of your earlier corrections were lost.
quiz.six-follow-ups.less-effort: The model gives less weight to short messages, so a series of separate asks is processed less accurately than 1 bundled instruction.
quiz.six-follow-ups.explanation: Rejected versions can remain in the request and distract the model despite their labels. Keep the current requirements clear and remove irrelevant history when needed.
quiz.reasoning-level.question: The agent reports a bug as fixed. Reading it back, you see it skipped a file and never ran the tests, although all the context was there. What do you change next time?
quiz.reasoning-level.effort: Raise the reasoning level, so the agent reads and checks more before it comes back.
quiz.reasoning-level.bigger-model: Pick a larger model, because a smarter model does not skip files.
quiz.reasoning-level.think-hard: Put "think hard" in your prompt, so the model thinks more thoroughly.
quiz.reasoning-level.bigger-window: Pick a model with a larger context, so all the files fit in it.
quiz.reasoning-level.explanation: Skipping a file or not running the tests is too little work, and that is what the reasoning level controls. A larger model helps only when the agent had all the context, clearly tried and was still wrong.
quiz.no-signal-in-the-answer.question: You want to check which of the 4 generated sentences come from files on disk. What do you base that check on?
quiz.no-signal-in-the-answer.nothing-doe: On what is actually in the context. The text of the answer does not settle it.
quiz.no-signal-in-the-answer.names-a-fil: On whether the wording names specific files.
quiz.no-signal-in-the-answer.hedged-ones: On how much doubt the sentences show, since hallucinations can be recognised by uncertain wording.
quiz.no-signal-in-the-answer.quoted-code: On whether the sentences quote the source code literally.
quiz.no-signal-in-the-answer.explanation: Inspect source content and tool results, then check that they support the claim. A citation or confident wording alone is not proof.
quiz.config-format-changed.question: The agent confidently names an option that was recently removed from a tool. How do you explain this behaviour?
quiz.config-format-changed.past-the-cuto: The change falls after the model's knowledge cutoff, so it falls back on older training data.
quiz.config-format-changed.knows-but-com: The model deliberately picks the most universal option across several versions.
quiz.config-format-changed.read-the-docs: The option was dug up from your command-line history from before the update.
quiz.config-format-changed.scores-higher: The removed option scores higher because it appears more often in the training data.
quiz.config-format-changed.explanation: After the cutoff there is nothing to be more or less sure about. The answer is the last version the model saw, delivered as surely as anything else it knows.
quiz.read-it-and-said-so.question: The agent read the test code and said the empty-list case was covered. In reality that test was missing. What explains this behaviour?
quiz.read-it-and-said-so.still-a-reading: The agent inferred the coverage from its reading, without naming the test and the assertion that check the case.
quiz.read-it-and-said-so.file-too-long: The relevant test fell outside the maximum length of the context.
quiz.read-it-and-said-so.after-cutoff: The file was too new for the model's knowledge cutoff.
quiz.read-it-and-said-so.nothing-in-wind: The model relied on recognition from its training data instead of the specific code.
quiz.read-it-and-said-so.explanation: Grounded is not proved. Running the tests would not have shown it, because a missing test never runs. Ask for the file and line of the test that covers the case, then run that test.
deck.tokens.split.title: A model does not read words
deck.tokens.split.note: In these samples, text and code use similar counts; a log line nearly 2 times as many, an id nearly 3 times.
deck.tokens.language.title: Token counts measure <hi>input size</hi>
deck.tokens.language.note: 10 tokens in English, 12 in Dutch for this sentence. Fragmentation alone does not establish answer quality.
deck.tokens.next.title: And it writes 1 token at a time
deck.tokens.attention.title: Each prediction depends on <hi>earlier context</hi>
deck.prompt.parts.title: How much <hi>1 prompt</hi> can carry
deck.prompt.bundle.title: 3 questions, or 1
deck.prompt.exact.title: Be exact about what changes
deck.prompt.plan.title: A reviewed plan makes <hi>requirements explicit</hi>
deck.tools.loop.title: An agent is a model <hi>in a loop</hi>
deck.tools.loop.note: It stops when the model asks for no more tools.
deck.tools.in-context.title: The tool runs outside the context
deck.tools.in-context.note: <hi>Execution outside the context:</hi> The harness runs the tool and adds the result to the context with a source label. <hi>Interpretation inside the model:</hi> Source labels give structure, but no guarantee that the model understands the result correctly.
deck.tools.mcp.title: 1 line, and what it carries lands in your context
deck.tools.parts.title: Sort them by who decides
deck.tools.list.title: Tool definitions take <hi>context space</hi>
deck.tools.list.1: <hi>The solution: Tool Search.</hi> Loads definitions only on demand, to save tokens with large toolboxes.
deck.tools.list.2: <hi>The warning: Context costs space.</hi> Every activated schema and every tool result keeps counting in the context.
deck.tools.list.3: <hi>The best practice: Pruning.</hi> Turn off everything that is not strictly needed for the current run.
deck.tools.injection.title: Tool results can contain <hi>unwanted instructions</hi>
deck.tools.injection.note: A ticket or web page can try to give the agent a different task. Check the source and review sensitive actions before approving them.
deck.tools.spot.title: Pick the odd one out
deck.tools.budget.title: Which 2 calls answer the question?
deck.context.diagram.title: Different sources, <hi>structured context</hi>
deck.context.stale.title: An outdated CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md misleads <hi>every session</hi>
deck.context.stale.note: It is read in at every start. Have the agent propose an edit whenever you contradict it.
deck.context.oneshot.title: Same prompt. 1 reference pinned.
deck.context.bad-code.title: Only a gate is <hi>certain</hi>
deck.context.bad-code.note: Per task you give the class, the scenario and the failing assertion. What always holds goes into the project: CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md, rules, and gates that fail when it goes wrong.
deck.context.data.title: Everything in the context <hi>leaves your machine</hi>
deck.context.data.note: Strip secrets and personal data before you paste. What the provider does with it depends on your plan.
deck.session.falloff.title: The model did not get tired. <hi>The evidence left the room.</hi>
deck.session.falloff.note: The result did not go wrong for lack of computing power, but because compaction summarised the crucial context away in a long conversation.
deck.session.entropy.title: Disorder grows every turn, unless you <hi>step in</hi>
deck.session.entropy.1: <hi>Context build-up:</hi> Stale data piles up quickly in between pruning and summarising.
deck.session.entropy.2: <hi>Symptoms:</hi> The agent contradicts itself, brings back an idea you rejected or an old version of a file.
deck.session.entropy.3: <hi>Active management:</hi> Without continuous cleanup, your agent's workspace inevitably gets polluted.
deck.session.makeup.title: 99.5% does <hi>not come from you</hi>
deck.session.clear.title: The one layer you can still <hi>throw away</hi>
deck.session.clear.note: <hi>The cost of compacting:</hi> Summarising, automatic or manual, costs both input and output tokens. <hi>/clear is free (immediately):</hi> It ends the history at once, without any summary request. <hi>The hidden cost:</hi> After a /clear you do have to build the context you need back up again.
deck.session.memory.title: The context is <hi>not your memory</hi>
deck.session.memory.note: Knowing what is in it right now, and being willing to throw it away, is most of what separates people who get work out of an agent from people who fight it.
deck.agent-patterns.decomposition.title: The human factor <hi>before</hi> the agent
deck.agent-patterns.decomposition.note: <hi>The prompt gap:</hi> What you actually ask for is always more concise than what you want in your head. <hi>Preparation on the board:</hi> Splitting the task happens in the analysis phase, before anyone opens an agent. <hi>Differences in interpretation:</hi> Without tight alignment, 3 developers build 3 different versions.
deck.agent-patterns.coordinator.title: The coordinator
deck.agent-patterns.coordinator.note: Fresh workers receive configured context and fetch relevant files. Forks can inherit history; worker models can be configured.
deck.agent-patterns.sequential.title: The sequential workflow
deck.agent-patterns.sequential.note: For steps that depend on each other. 1 session carries the whole run, so a long workflow is a full context by the end.
deck.agent-patterns.reflection.title: Reflection
deck.agent-patterns.reflection.note: A separate brief can reduce anchoring. Give the critic requirements and evidence, and verify its findings.
deck.agent-patterns.routing.title: Sort first, <hi>then</hi> send
deck.agent-patterns.routing.note: Your harness already routes by description. Jev answers a routing question with a choice and a probability, and plain code checks it before the model is switched.
deck.tokens.cache.title: The cache is a <hi>prefix match</hi> from the first byte
deck.tokens.cache.note: Changing an early prefix can invalidate what follows. TTL and rates depend on provider and configuration; inspect reported usage.
deck.agent-patterns.patterns.title: Which pattern fits?
deck.model.tiers.title: 1 family, <hi>different task candidates</hi>
deck.model.pricing.title: 1, 2 and 4
deck.model.pricing.note: These ratios and prices are dated. Recheck them for the model and provider you use.
deck.model.money.title: Cumulative usage, <hi>separate from capacity</hi>
deck.model.money.1: <hi>Measure the real cost:</hi> Read /usage over several requests for a realistic picture of usage.
deck.model.money.2: <hi>Differentiated rates:</hi> Input, cache reads, cache writes and output each have their own price.
deck.model.money.3: <hi>Capacity vs. invoice:</hi> Room for a large context costs nothing by itself; you pay only for the tokens actually processed.
deck.model.speed.title: Where <hi>quick</hi> stops being cheap
deck.model.speed.1: <hi>The golden triangle:</hi> Always measure the balance between quality, latency (waiting time) and token cost on representative tasks.
deck.model.speed.2: <hi>Relative speeds:</hi> Processing times (such as seconds in a benchmark) are examples, not fixed speed guarantees.
deck.model.speed.3: <hi>Trade-off:</hi> Speed and computing power do not scale linearly; pick the 'sweet spot' for your specific use case.
deck.model.billing.title: API costs vs. <hi>subscription limits</hi>
deck.model.billing.1: <hi>Look at tokens:</hi> Always read the hard usage figures, not the estimated dollars.
deck.model.billing.2: <hi>2 separate worlds:</hi> An API calculation does not reflect the fixed costs or limits of your subscription.
deck.model.billing.3: <hi>Keep control:</hi> Use measured data to manage both your budget and your rate limits.
deck.model.reasoning.title: Effort is <hi>not the same</hi> as the tier
deck.model.reasoning.1: <hi>Model tier (which model):</hi> Decides the fundamental capability of the engine.
deck.model.reasoning.2: <hi>Effort / reasoning (how thorough):</hi> Decides how much time and how many thinking tokens the model spends on the task.
deck.model.reasoning.3: <hi>Key insight:</hi> Turning on more reasoning time does not make a lighter model a heavier one.
deck.model.pick.title: Which tier would you run?
deck.truth.sounds-same.title: Certainty says <hi>nothing</hi>
deck.truth.sounds-same.1: <hi>No difference:</hi> Facts, context and hallucinations sound equally convincing.
deck.truth.sounds-same.2: <hi>The pitfall:</hi> Trusting the tone instead of the reasoning behind it.
deck.truth.sounds-same.3: <hi>What to do:</hi> Always ask where the answer comes from and how it was verified.
deck.truth.grounded.title: Same question, <mute>2 contexts</mute>
deck.truth.provenance.title: 1 answer, and only some of it was <hi>read</hi>
deck.truth.proof.title: A test that goes red is <hi>a claim that can fail</hi>
deck.truth.proof.1: <hi>Asking the agent:</hi> "Does this work with an empty list?" → You trust the agent's reading.
deck.truth.proof.2: <hi>Running a test:</hi> Run the test with an empty list → You trust the machine.
deck.truth.proof.3: <hi>Core rule:</hi> Replace the model's assumptions with verifiable test results.
deck.workshop.flags.title: 5 flags, 5 places an answer can come from
deck.workshop.flags.note: Ask what your machine told it, read the response, turn the log level up, read the source, trace the run.
deck.workshop.debrief.title: Which flag could you have <hi>handed over whole</hi>?
deck.recap.one-window.title: The mechanisms behind <hi>each request</hi>
deck.recap.one-window.note: What fills it, what it costs and who reads it.
deck.recap.moves.title: Keep context relevant and <hi>verify the result</hi>
deck.recap.moves.note: Paste only what matters, bundle, clear at your own seam, turn off what you do not need, keep secrets out.
deck.recap.next.title: Step 2: how you <hi>hand it work</hi>
deck.recap.next.note: Keep the context in mind there.
deck.tokens.tokenizer.title: Text in, <hi>numbers</hi> out
deck.tokens.network.title: Numbers in → <hi>Probabilities</hi> out
deck.tokens.sampling.title: Settings decide <hi>how widely it picks</hi>
deck.tokens.sampling.note: You do not set them yourself: the newest Claude models accept only the default values.
deck.tokens.pick.title: What are the possible next tokens?
deck.tokens.kinds.title: Output tokens <hi>cost more</hi>
deck.tokens.kinds.note: The turn is made up. The ratios between the kinds are not.
deck.tokens.divider.1: <hi>Tokenisation:</hi> Text is cut up according to a fixed, frozen vocabulary.
deck.tokens.divider.2: <hi>Token density:</hi> The number of tokens varies with the type of text and the tokeniser chosen.
deck.tokens.divider.3: <hi>Generation:</hi> Every new token is worked out from the full context before it.
deck.prompt.divider.1: <hi>Layers of instruction:</hi> The prompt is the smallest layer, and the layer that carries the intent.
deck.prompt.divider.2: <hi>Purpose of reasoning:</hi> Use reasoning for complex tasks, not to make up for vague prompts.
deck.prompt.divider.3: <hi>Sharp scoping:</hi> Bundle related questions and be exact about what needs to change.
deck.prompt.reasoning.title: Effort guides <hi>thoroughness</hi>
deck.prompt.reasoning.1: <hi>Complexity:</hi> On a hard question the model thinks it through more deeply.
deck.prompt.reasoning.2: <hi>No mind reading:</hi> What you leave out of the prompt, reasoning does not fill in for you.
deck.prompt.reasoning.3: <hi>Cost:</hi> Every thinking token (reasoning token) counts as output on the bill.
deck.prompt.meta.title: Let <hi>the expensive model</hi> write the prompt
deck.prompt.meta.1: <hi>Small investment:</hi> A good prompt costs only a few hundred tokens.
deck.prompt.meta.2: <hi>Big saving:</hi> The real money goes into actually running the task.
deck.prompt.meta.3: <hi>The gain:</hi> A sharp prompt prevents expensive, wrong runs afterwards.
deck.tools.divider.1: <hi>External execution:</hi> The tool runs outside the model; the result lands inside as context.
deck.tools.divider.2: <hi>Context budget:</hi> Even unused tool definitions take up valuable context space.
deck.tools.divider.3: <hi>Information vs. instruction:</hi> Treat tool results as facts/data, not new commands.
deck.context.divider.2: Wrong context is worse than missing context
deck.session.divider.1: <hi>State management:</hi> The session is the only layer that actually keeps a history.
deck.session.divider.2: <hi>Your share:</hi> In the example, only half a percent of the tokens in the context comes from your own keyboard.
deck.session.divider.3: <hi>Cost focus:</hi> The length and duration of sessions decide by far the largest part of your total token budget.
deck.agent-patterns.divider.1: <hi>Patterns:</hi> Cut the task, hand it out, run it in steps, have it criticised, route it.
deck.agent-patterns.divider.2: <hi>Context handover:</hi> Decide deliberately which history and instructions each worker inherits.
deck.agent-patterns.divider.3: <hi>Routing:</hi> A small model can decide which model, skill or agent gets the request.
deck.model.divider.1: <hi>Tiers:</hi> Model tiers step up in price (1× → 2× → 4×).
deck.model.divider.2: <hi>Ratio:</hi> Output costs ~5× the price of input.
deck.model.divider.3: <hi>Selection:</hi> Do not choose on gut feeling, but on task-specific measurements.
deck.truth.divider.1: <hi>3 sources of knowledge:</hi> Information is trained (memory), handed over (context) or discovered (tools).
deck.truth.divider.2: <hi>The pitfall:</hi> The model sounds just as convincing and sure of itself with all 3 sources.
deck.truth.divider.3: <hi>The solution:</hi> Ask the model for the reasoning and the check, not just for the conclusion.
deck.workshop.divider.1: <hi>Focused scope:</hi> 5 flags to track down, 4 of them from 1 specific service.
deck.workshop.divider.2: <hi>End-to-end measurement:</hi> 1 single session, monitored and measured at both the start and the finish line.
deck.workshop.divider.3: <hi>Full autonomy:</hi> Only the agent does the searching; you do not read the code yourself.
deck.recap.divider.1: <hi>Know and do:</hi> every unit left 1 thing to know and 1 move to make.
deck.recap.divider.2: <hi>Shared space:</hi> All interactions, history and tool outputs share one and the same context.
deck.recap.divider.3: What you learned here <hi>still holds</hi> in step 2
